topics.title: Strain energy, dissociation and stacking faults

questions.text: Match the defect dimension to its class.
tableRows: (b) grain boundaries, twin boundaries, stacking faults
questions.keyExplanation: 1-c (0-D point), 2-a (1-D line), 3-b (2-D planar), 4-d (3-D volume).
questions.concise: 0-D point · 1-D line · 2-D planar · 3-D volume.
questions.detailed:
| Dimension | Class | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **0-D** | Point defects | vacancies, interstitials, substitutional solute atoms |
| **1-D** | Line defects | dislocations |
| **2-D** | Planar defects | grain boundaries, twin boundaries, stacking faults |
| **3-D** | Volume defects | voids, cracks, inclusions, precipitates |

The classification is by the defect's *dimensionality* — how many directions it is extended
along. Vacancies are 0-D because they are localised to a single site; a dislocation is 1-D
because it is extended along a line.

questions.text: Which statement(s) about real crystals is/are correct?

statements.text: Real crystals always contain defects.
It is the defects — not perfect bonding — that control strength, ductility, diffusion and corrosion.
A perfectly defect-free crystal is what every engineering metal actually is.
Point defects enable diffusion.

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2, 4 correct; item 3 is the idealisation that is never true of engineering metals.
questions.concise: Real crystals always contain defects, and it is the defects that control the properties — no engineering metal is defect-free.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: real crystals always contain defects.
- Item 2 — TRUE: it is the defects — not perfect bonding — that control strength, ductility,
  diffusion and corrosion.
- Item 3 — FALSE: a perfectly defect-free crystal is an idealisation; no engineering metal is
  one. (If it were, it would be astronomically strong — see Q13/Q15.)
- Item 4 — TRUE: point defects (vacancies) enable diffusion.
Item 3 is the false member, and it is contradicted by item 1 within the same question.

questions.text: Volume (3-D) defects include:

statements.text: voids  2. cracks  3. inclusions and precipitates  4. vacancies

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2, 3 correct; vacancies are 0-D point defects, not volume defects.
questions.concise: Voids, cracks, inclusions and precipitates are 3-D; vacancies are 0-D point defects.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: voids.
- Item 2 — TRUE: cracks.
- Item 3 — TRUE: inclusions and precipitates.
- Item 4 — FALSE: vacancies are **0-D point** defects, not volume defects.
Items 1–3 are all extended in three dimensions; a vacancy is confined to a single lattice site.

questions.text: A *vacancy* is:

options.label: a
options.text: a missing atom at a normal lattice site

options.label: b
options.text: an extra atom squeezed between normal sites

options.label: c
options.text: a foreign atom replacing a host atom

questions.keyExplanation: [P2] Vacancy = atom *missing from a site*.
questions.concise: Vacancy = atom *missing from a site*.
questions.detailed:
A **vacancy** is an empty lattice site — an atom missing from its normal position.
- (b) describes a **self-interstitial** (Q5).
- (c) describes a **substitutional** solute.
- (d) describes a **dislocation** (missing plane, a 1-D defect).
**[P2] rule:** *vacancy = missing from a site; interstitial = extra between sites.* Say it once.

questions.text: A *self-interstitial* is:

options.label: a
options.text: a missing atom at a lattice site

options.label: b
options.text: a host atom squeezed into a non-lattice interstitial site — high strain energy, low concentration

options.label: c
options.text: a foreign atom at a lattice site

options.label: d
options.text: an atom at a grain boundary

questions.keyExplanation: [P2] Interstitial = extra atom *squeezed between sites*; high strain energy, low concentration.
questions.concise: Self-interstitial = host atom between sites; high strain energy, so low concentration.
questions.detailed:
A **self-interstitial** is a host atom displaced into a non-lattice (interstitial)
position. Because it does not fit in the small void, it creates a **large strain field**, which
means a **high formation energy** — so its equilibrium concentration is very low compared to
vacancies.
- (a) describes a vacancy.
- (c) a foreign atom at a lattice site is a *substitutional solute*.
- (d) is not a point-defect classification.
The pairing to remember: vacancies are common (Q8), self-interstitials are rare — because of the
strain energy.

questions.text: Which statement(s) distinguish a *Frenkel* defect from a *Schottky* defect?

statements.text: In a Frenkel defect, the displaced ion moves to an interstitial site **within the same crystal** — no mass loss.
In a Schottky defect, a stoichiometric ion pair leaves the crystal entirely — a mass/density change results.
A Frenkel defect produces a measurable density change.
Both involve an ion leaving the crystal.

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2 correct. Item 3 is false — Frenkel involves no mass loss, so no density change. [P2]
questions.concise: Frenkel = ion moves to an interstitial *within* the crystal (no mass loss); Schottky = a stoichiometric ion pair *leaves* (density change).
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: in a **Frenkel** defect the displaced ion moves to an interstitial site *within
  the same crystal* — no mass loss, no density change.
- Item 2 — TRUE: in a **Schottky** defect a stoichiometric ion pair *leaves* the crystal entirely
  — a mass/density change results.
- Item 3 — FALSE: a Frenkel defect produces **no** density change (nothing left the crystal).
- Item 4 — FALSE: in a Frenkel defect the ion stays *inside*; it does not leave.
**[P2] rule — the distinguishing question:** *does the ion stay in the crystal (Frenkel, no mass
change) or leave (Schottky, density change)?* Items 3 and 4 both wrongly ascribe the Schottky
behaviour to the Frenkel case.

questions.text: The equilibrium vacancy concentration is given by:
questions.keyExplanation: n_v/N = exp(−Q_v/kT).
questions.concise: n_v/N = exp(−Q_v/kT).
questions.detailed:
The equilibrium vacancy fraction is:
```
n_v / N = exp( −Q_v / kT )
```
where Q_v = vacancy formation energy (per atom), k = Boltzmann's constant (8.62 × 10⁻⁵ eV/K),
T = absolute temperature (K).
- (b) has the wrong sign — a positive exponent would give an ever-growing, unbounded concentration.
- (c), (d) are not exponential forms.
This is a Boltzmann distribution: the probability of paying an energy cost Q_v in thermal
fluctuations at temperature T.

questions.text: For copper (Q_v = 0.9 eV/atom, k = 8.62 × 10⁻⁵ eV/K) at T = 1000 K, the vacancy fraction n_v/N is approximately:
questions.detailed:
```
Q_v = 0.9 eV,  k = 8.62 × 10⁻⁵ eV/K,  T = 1000 K

exponent = −Q_v/(kT)
         = −0.9 / (8.62 × 10⁻⁵ × 1000)
         = −0.9 / 0.0862
         = −10.44

n_v/N = exp(−10.44) ≈ 2.9 × 10⁻⁵
```
- (a) 2.9 × 10⁻² would require an exponent of ≈ −3.5.
- (c) 2.9 × 10⁻⁹ would require an exponent of ≈ −19.3.
- (d) 1.0 × 10⁻³ is not this result.
**Watch the units:** k must be in eV/K to match Q_v in eV — using J/K is the classic slip.

questions.text: The result of Q8 corresponds to roughly one vacant site in every:
questions.detailed:
```
1 / (2.9 × 10⁻⁵) = 34,483 ≈ 34,000 sites
```
So at 1000 K roughly **one lattice site in every 34,000** is vacant.
- (a) 340 and (b) 3,400 correspond to 10× and 100× larger fractions.
- (d) 340,000 corresponds to a 10× smaller fraction.
The striking point: even in a *perfect-looking* crystal at high temperature, a measurable
fraction of sites are empty — and this is what makes solid-state diffusion (Ch. 8) possible.

questions.assertion: Vacancy concentration rises exponentially with temperature.
questions.reason: Q_v/kT falls as T rises, so exp(−Q_v/kT) grows rapidly.

options.label: a
options.text: Both true, R correctly explains A

options.label: b
options.text: Both true, R does not explain A

questions.keyExplanation: Both true — the exponential dependence on 1/T.
questions.concise: Q_v/kT falls as T rises, so exp(−Q_v/kT) grows rapidly.
questions.detailed:
- A is TRUE: vacancy concentration rises exponentially with temperature.
- R is TRUE: the exponent −Q_v/kT becomes *less negative* as T rises (Q_v/kT falls), so
  exp(−Q_v/kT) grows rapidly.

R correctly explains A. The exponential dependence is why vacancies are negligible at room
temperature but abundant near the melting point — and why quenching (Q11) is such a powerful
way to trap them.

questions.text: Quenching a metal from high temperature is an effective way to supersaturate it with vacancies because:

statements.text: the high-temperature equilibrium vacancy population is "frozen in"
the vacancy concentration falls by orders of magnitude at room temperature
rapid cooling gives no time for vacancies to migrate to sinks
quenching creates vacancies by breaking bonds at the surface

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2, 3 correct; item 4 is not the mechanism (quenching *traps* existing vacancies).
questions.concise: Quenching traps the high-T equilibrium population; the RT concentration is far lower, and rapid cooling gives no time for vacancies to reach sinks.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: the high-temperature equilibrium vacancy population is "frozen in".
- Item 2 — TRUE: the vacancy concentration falls by orders of magnitude at room temperature (Q10).
- Item 3 — TRUE: rapid cooling gives no time for vacancies to migrate to sinks (grain boundaries,
  surfaces, dislocations) where they would be annihilated.
- Item 4 — FALSE: quenching does **not** create vacancies by breaking surface bonds — it *traps*
  the vacancies that already existed in equilibrium at high temperature.
Item 4 is the false member: quenching preserves, rather than generates, the vacancy population.
The result is a **supersaturation** of vacancies, which then provides the driving force for
precipitation (Ch. 7) and can be measured electrically.

questions.text: Frenkel's sinusoidal shear model gives a restoring stress:
questions.keyExplanation: τ = τ_max sin(2πx/b), a sinusoidal restoring stress.
questions.concise: Frenkel model: sinusoidal restoring stress with period b.
questions.detailed:
Frenkel modelled two adjacent atomic planes sheared relative to one another by x,
with atomic periodicity b along the shear direction. The restoring shear stress is periodic in x
with period b, so it is approximated by:
```
τ = τ_max sin( 2πx / b )
```
- (b) a cosine would not vanish at x = 0 (where the crystal is unstressed) — wrong phase.
- (c) τ = Gx/a is only the *small-x* linear approximation, not the full periodic form.
- (d) is not the expression.
The sinusoid is the key: it allows a *finite maximum* stress, which is what makes a theoretical
strength calculable at all.

questions.text: The Frenkel estimate of the theoretical shear strength is:
questions.keyExplanation: τ_max ≈ Gb/2πa ≈ G/2π ≈ 0.16 G.
questions.concise: Frenkel: τ_max ≈ Gb/2πa ≈ G/2π ≈ 0.16G.
questions.detailed:
Matching the two small-x expressions:
```
sin θ ≈ θ  gives   τ_max · 2πx/b  ≈  Gx/a        (since G = τ/γ, γ = x/a)

⇒  τ_max ≈ Gb/(2πa)

taking b ≈ a:
⇒  τ_max ≈ G/2π ≈ 0.16 G
```
- (b) G/1000 and (c) G/100,000 are *experimental* strengths, not theoretical.
- (d) 2πG would be larger than the shear modulus — physically impossible.
So the naive theory says a perfect crystal should withstand ~16% of its shear modulus in shear.

questions.text: Using more realistic interatomic potentials lowers the theoretical estimate to roughly:
questions.keyExplanation: Realistic potentials bring it to ≈ G/30.
questions.concise: Realistic interatomic potentials lower the estimate to ≈ G/30.
questions.detailed:
Replacing Frenkel's sine with a more realistic interatomic potential (which gives a
broader, lower maximum) lowers the theoretical estimate to roughly:
```
τ_theoretical ≈ G/30
```
- (b) G/3 would be far too high.
- (c) G/3000 is too low (closer to real than to theory).
This refined figure is still ~30× the strength of a real single crystal (Q15) — the gap that
demands dislocations exist.

questions.text: Real metal single crystals yield at shear stresses of about:

options.label: a
options.text: G/1000 to G/100,000 — three to four orders of magnitude below the theoretical value

questions.keyExplanation: G/1000 to G/100,000 — the gap that demands dislocations exist. [P2]
questions.concise: Real crystals yield at G/1000–G/100,000, i.e. 3–4 orders below theory.
questions.detailed:
Real metal single crystals yield at shear stresses of about:
```
τ_actual ≈ G/1000  to  G/100,000
```
Compare: theoretical ≈ G/30 (Q14) or G/2π (Q13). So the discrepancy is **three to four orders
of magnitude**.
- (b) G/2π and (c) G/30 are the *theoretical* values.
- (d) is the opposite of the truth.
**[P2] rule:** *theoretical strength ≈ G/30 to G/2π; actual strength ≈ G/1000 to G/100,000.*
Mixing these two families is the classic error.

questions.text: The huge discrepancy between theoretical and actual strength was recognised independently in 1934 by:

statements.text: Taylor  2. Orowan  3. Polanyi  4. Frenkel

questions.keyExplanation: Taylor, Orowan and Polanyi, 1934. (Frenkel made the *theoretical* estimate, not the dislocation proposal.)
questions.concise: Taylor, Orowan and Polanyi, independently in 1934.
questions.detailed:
The recognition that real crystals must contain a mobile defect came independently
in **1934** from:
- **Taylor** — introduced dislocation motion and strain hardening
- **Orowan** — connected dislocations to plasticity and creep
- **Polanyi** — proposed edge dislocations in ionic crystals
- (4) **Frenkel** made the *theoretical strength estimate* (Q12–Q13), not the dislocation
  proposal — this is the distractor.
All three proposed essentially the same entity (the dislocation) to explain the strength
discrepancy.

questions.assertion: Real metals are far weaker than theory predicts.
questions.reason: Crystals already contain dislocations, and slip proceeds by moving a dislocation through the crystal — breaking and re-forming only one row of bonds at a time at the core, rather than every bond across the whole plane simultaneously.

options.label: a
options.text: Both true, R correctly explains A

options.label: b
options.text: Both true, R does not explain A

questions.keyExplanation: Both true — one row of bonds at a time, not the whole plane.
questions.concise: Slip proceeds by moving a dislocation, breaking one row of bonds at a time rather than the whole plane.
questions.detailed:
- A is TRUE: real metals are far weaker than theory predicts.
- R is TRUE: crystals already contain dislocations, and slip proceeds by moving a dislocation
  through the crystal — breaking and re-forming only **one row of bonds at a time** at the core,
  rather than every bond across the whole plane simultaneously.

R correctly explains A. This is the central insight of dislocation theory: the *mechanism* is
step-wise rather than collective, so the required stress drops from G/30 to G/1000–G/100,000.
Think of moving a carpet wrinkle rather than dragging the whole carpet.

questions.text: An edge dislocation is:

options.label: a
options.text: the edge of an extra half-plane of atoms inserted partway into the crystal, denoted ⊥

options.label: b
options.text: a helical ramp of planes around a line

questions.keyExplanation: Extra half-plane of atoms, denoted ⊥.
questions.concise: Edge = extra half-plane of atoms, denoted ⊥.
questions.detailed:
An **edge dislocation** is the edge of an extra half-plane of atoms inserted
partway into the crystal. It is denoted **⊥**, where the vertical stroke is the extra half-plane
and the horizontal stroke is the slip plane.
- (b) describes a *screw* dislocation (Q19).
- (c) a missing plane is not the standard description.
- (d) is a planar defect, not a line defect.

questions.text: A screw dislocation forms when:

options.label: a
options.text: one part of a crystal is sheared relative to the rest parallel to the dislocation line, so planes spiral like a screw thread

options.label: c
options.text: a vacancy migrates to the surface

questions.keyExplanation: Shear parallel to the line → helical ramp.
questions.concise: Screw = shear parallel to the line → helical ramp of planes.
questions.detailed:
A **screw dislocation** forms when one part of a crystal is sheared relative to
the rest **parallel to the dislocation line**. The lattice planes are no longer flat but form a
single helical ramp around the line, like the thread of a screw.
- (b) describes an *edge* dislocation.
- (c) describes vacancy migration (diffusion).
- (d) describes a twin or recrystallisation.
**The discriminating test:** is the shear *perpendicular* to the line (edge) or *parallel* (screw)?

questions.text: Which statement(s) about the *edge* dislocation is/are correct?

statements.text: The Burgers vector is perpendicular to the dislocation line.
The slip plane is unique (it contains both b and the line).
It can climb, which requires vacancy diffusion.
It can cross-slip.

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2, 3 correct. Item 4 is **false** — edge dislocations cannot cross-slip. [P2]
questions.concise: Edge: b ⊥ line, unique slip plane, can climb — but **cannot** cross-slip.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: for an edge dislocation the Burgers vector is **perpendicular** to the line.
- Item 2 — TRUE: the slip plane is unique — it is the plane containing both **b** and the line
  direction (the plane of the extra half-plane).
- Item 3 — TRUE: it can **climb**, which requires vacancy diffusion (Q27).
- Item 4 — FALSE: **cross-slip is a screw capability**, not an edge one. Because the edge has a
  unique slip plane (item 2), there is nowhere to cross-slip *to*.
Item 4 is a [P2] cross-contamination — the screw's ability transplanted onto the edge. Note that
items 2 and 4 are mutually inconsistent: a unique slip plane makes cross-slip impossible.

questions.text: Which statement(s) about the *screw* dislocation is/are correct?

statements.text: The Burgers vector is parallel to the dislocation line.
It may lie in any plane containing that line, so it has no unique slip plane.
It can cross-slip, and this needs no diffusion.
It has both a shear and a hydrostatic strain component.

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2, 3 correct. Item 4 is **false** — a screw has a *pure shear* field; the hydrostatic component belongs to edge. [P2]
questions.concise: Screw: b ∥ line, any plane containing the line, can cross-slip — but its strain field is **pure shear**, not shear + hydrostatic.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: for a screw dislocation the Burgers vector is **parallel** to the line.
- Item 2 — TRUE: it may lie in *any* plane containing that line, so it has **no unique slip plane**.
- Item 3 — TRUE: it can **cross-slip**, and this needs no diffusion (a purely conservative motion).
- Item 4 — FALSE: a screw has a **pure shear** strain field with **no hydrostatic component**.
  The hydrostatic (compression/tension) component belongs to the *edge* dislocation.
Item 4 is the [P2] trap. The reason is geometric: a screw has no extra half-plane, so there is no
region of compression or tension — only shear. This is the concept flagged as "most-missed" in
the chapter.

questions.text: Just above an edge dislocation's extra half-plane the lattice is in:
questions.keyExplanation: Compression above (where the extra half-plane crowds the lattice).
questions.concise: Above the extra half-plane the lattice is in compression.
questions.detailed:
The extra half-plane of an edge dislocation crowds the lattice **above** it (on the
side the half-plane is inserted from), so the atoms there are squeezed closer together —
**compression**.
- (b) tension occurs *below* (Q23).
- (c), (d) are wrong for this region.
This compression/tension pair is what gives the edge dislocation its hydrostatic component (and
is why interstitial solutes segregate below the plane — Ch. 6 Q34).

questions.text: Just below an edge dislocation's extra half-plane the lattice is in:
questions.keyExplanation: Tension below.
questions.concise: Below the extra half-plane the lattice is in tension.
questions.detailed:
Below the extra half-plane there is a "missing" row of atoms, so the surrounding
atoms are pulled apart — **tension**.
- (a) compression occurs *above* (Q22).
Together: **compression above, tension below**. This asymmetric field is:
- why the screw is contrasted as pure-shear (Q21),
- why carbon/nitrogen segregate into the tensile zone to form Cottrell atmospheres (Ch. 6).

questions.text: Match the property to the dislocation type.
tableRows: b ⊥ line; unique slip plane; can climb
b ∥ line; any plane containing the line; can cross-slip
questions.keyExplanation: 1-b, 2-a, 3-a (screw = pure shear), 4-b (edge = shear + hydrostatic).
questions.concise: b⊥ line/unique plane/climb = edge · b∥ line/any plane/cross-slip = screw · pure shear = screw · shear+hydrostatic = edge.
questions.detailed:
| Feature | Type |
|---|---|
| b ⊥ line; unique slip plane; can climb | **edge** |
| b ∥ line; any plane containing the line; can cross-slip | **screw** |
| Pure shear strain field | **screw** |
| Both shear and hydrostatic components | **edge** |

The complete comparison table for the two dislocation types:
| | Edge | Screw |
|---|---|---|
| b vs line | perpendicular | parallel |
| Symbol | ⊥ | — |
| Slip plane | **unique** | any plane containing line |
| Extra motion | **climb** (needs vacancies) | **cross-slip** (no diffusion) |
| Strain field | shear **+ hydrostatic** | **pure shear** |

Learn this table as one unit and Q20, Q21, Q24, Q41 all collapse into recall.

questions.text: Most dislocations in real crystals are perfectly pure edge or pure screw.

options.label: b
options.text: False — most are mixed, with edge and screw character varying continuously along a curved line

questions.keyExplanation: Most are mixed; pure edge or pure screw only at points/special cases.
questions.concise: Most real dislocations are *mixed*, not pure edge or pure screw.
questions.detailed:
**False.** A dislocation line that is not straight generally changes character
along its length — it may be pure edge at one point, pure screw at another, and mixed in between.
Because a Burgers vector is fixed for a given dislocation but the line direction varies, the
fraction of edge vs screw character varies continuously around a curved loop (as in an expanding
Frank–Read loop, Q42).

questions.reason: Their slip plane is uniquely fixed by the Burgers vector and the line direction, so there is no second plane available.

options.label: a
options.text: Both true, R correctly explains A

options.label: b
options.text: Both true, R does not explain A

questions.keyExplanation: Both true — unique slip plane means nowhere to cross-slip to.
questions.concise: Unique slip plane (set by b and the line) means there is no second plane to move to.
questions.detailed:
- A is TRUE: edge dislocations cannot cross-slip.
- R is TRUE: their slip plane is uniquely fixed by the Burgers vector and the line direction
  (the plane containing both), so there is no second plane available for them to move onto.

R correctly explains A. Contrast with the screw (Q21): because b ∥ line for a screw, there are
*infinitely many* planes containing both, so it can choose. This is exactly why the geometry of
b determines the available motion.

questions.assertion: Climb is a non-conservative, thermally activated process that is negligible at room temperature.
questions.reason: Climb requires the extra half-plane to absorb or emit a row of vacancies, which involves long-range vacancy diffusion.

options.label: a
options.text: Both true, R correctly explains A

options.label: b
options.text: Both true, R does not explain A

questions.keyExplanation: Both true — climb needs vacancy diffusion, hence thermally activated.
questions.concise: Climb needs the half-plane to absorb/emit vacancies, which requires long-range vacancy diffusion.
questions.detailed:
- A is TRUE: climb is a non-conservative, thermally activated process that is negligible at room temperature.
- R is TRUE: climb requires the extra half-plane to absorb or emit a row of vacancies, which
  involves long-range **vacancy diffusion**.

R correctly explains A. Three linked properties follow from the diffusion requirement:
1. it needs **vacancies** → edge only (screw has no half-plane to absorb/emits);
2. it is **non-conservative** (the dislocation moves out of its slip plane);
3. it is **thermally activated** → negligible at room T, important in creep (Ch. 7) and recovery.

questions.text: The Burgers vector b is found as:

options.label: a
options.text: the closure failure of an atomic circuit drawn around the dislocation in the real crystal, compared with the same circuit in a perfect reference crystal, measured Finish to Start (FS/RH)

options.label: b
options.text: the distance between two unit cells

options.label: d
options.text: the length of the dislocation line

questions.keyExplanation: Closure failure, FS/RH convention.
questions.concise: b = closure failure of a circuit around the dislocation, FS/RH convention.
questions.detailed:
To find the Burgers vector:
1. Draw an atomic circuit around the dislocation in the **real** crystal, using the same number
   of atomic steps in each direction — this will **not close** (closure failure).
2. Draw the identical circuit in a **perfect reference crystal** — it *does* close.
3. The vector needed to close the real circuit, drawn **Finish → Start** (FS) using the
   **right-hand (RH)** convention, is **b**.
- (b), (c), (d) are not the definition; b is not the cell edge, the interplanar spacing, or the
  line length.

questions.text: Which statement(s) about the Burgers vector is/are correct?

statements.text: Its magnitude and direction fix the slip direction.
Its magnitude fixes the dislocation strain energy (∝ b²).
It connects two nearest-neighbour atoms along the close-packed direction.
It is always parallel to the dislocation line.

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2, 3 correct; item 4 is only true for *screw* dislocations. [P2]
questions.concise: b fixes slip direction, strain energy (∝ b²) and connects nearest neighbours along the close-packed direction — but it is not always parallel to the line.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: its magnitude and direction fix the slip direction.
- Item 2 — TRUE: its magnitude fixes the dislocation strain energy (∝ b²).
- Item 3 — TRUE: it connects two nearest-neighbour atoms along the close-packed direction.
- Item 4 — FALSE: b is parallel to the line **only for a screw** dislocation; for an edge it is
  perpendicular (Q20, Q24).
Item 4 is a [P2] over-generalisation from the screw case.

questions.text: The Burgers vector and its magnitude for BCC are:
questions.concise: BCC: b = a/2⟨111⟩, magnitude (√3/2)a.
questions.detailed:
```
BCC:  b = (a/2)⟨111⟩     e.g. b = (a/2)[111]
      |b| = (a/2)√(1²+1²+1²) = (a/2)√3 = (√3/2) a ≈ 0.866 a
```
- (b) a/2⟨110⟩ is the **FCC** Burgers vector (Q31).
- (c) a⟨100⟩ is the **simple cubic** vector (Q32).
- (d) a/6⟨112⟩ is a **partial (Shockley)** vector.
In BCC the closest lattice translation is along the body diagonal ⟨111⟩ — consistent with atoms
touching along that diagonal (Ch. 2 Q10).

questions.text: The Burgers vector and its magnitude for FCC are:
questions.keyExplanation: FCC: b = a/2⟨110⟩, |b| = a/√2. [P2] — do not swap these two.
questions.concise: FCC: b = a/2⟨110⟩, magnitude a/√2.
questions.detailed:
```
FCC:  b = (a/2)⟨110⟩     e.g. b = (a/2)[110]
      |b| = (a/2)√(1²+1²+0²) = (a/2)√2 = a/√2 ≈ 0.707 a
```
- (a) a/2⟨111⟩ is the **BCC** vector (Q30).
- (c) a⟨100⟩ is simple cubic.
- (d) a/4⟨111⟩ is not a valid FCC lattice translation (would not map the lattice onto itself).
**Q30 and Q31 are the classic [P2] swap.** The test: FCC's closest translation runs along a
*face* diagonal ⟨110⟩ (atoms touch along faces); BCC's runs along the *body* diagonal ⟨111⟩
(atoms touch along the body diagonal). Derive them from the contact direction rather than
memorising blindly.

questions.text: For simple cubic, b = a⟨100⟩ with |b| = a. This is consistent with the rule that nature always picks:

options.label: b
options.text: the smallest possible lattice translation that maps the lattice onto itself, because strain energy grows with b²

options.label: d
options.text: the Burgers vector perpendicular to the close-packed direction

questions.keyExplanation: Smallest translation, because E ∝ b².
questions.concise: Nature always picks the smallest valid translation, since E ∝ b².
questions.detailed:
The guiding rule for the Burgers vector: **always the smallest possible lattice
translation** that maps the crystal onto itself. Simple cubic has its nearest neighbours a
distance *a* apart along ⟨100⟩, so b = a⟨100⟩ with |b| = a is the shortest valid choice.
- (a) the largest available b would maximise strain energy — the opposite of what happens.
- (c) b is not random; it is fixed by the lattice geometry.
- (d) b always lies *along* the close-packed direction (Q29), not perpendicular.
The b² energy dependence (Q34) is what enforces this: splitting into smaller vectors is always
favoured if possible.

questions.assertion: In every crystal structure, the Burgers vector connects two nearest-neighbour atoms along the close-packed direction.
questions.reason: Strain energy scales as b², so the smallest available translation is always the energetically preferred one.

options.label: a
options.text: Both true, R correctly explains A

options.label: b
options.text: Both true, R does not explain A

questions.keyExplanation: Both true — b² energy cost is the reason.
questions.concise: Strain energy scales as b², so the smallest available translation is always preferred.
questions.detailed:
- A is TRUE: in every structure the Burgers vector connects two nearest-neighbour atoms along
  the close-packed direction.
- R is TRUE: strain energy scales as **b²**, so the smallest available translation is always the
  energetically preferred one — and the closest-neighbour distance along the close-packed
  direction *is* that smallest translation.

R correctly explains A. This one rule explains the b values in Q30, Q31 and Q32 without any
memorisation, and it also explains why dislocations dissociate (Q35).

questions.text: The dislocation strain energy per unit length is approximately:

options.label: a
options.text: E ≈ αGb², with α ≈ ½ to 1

questions.keyExplanation: E ≈ αGb², α ≈ ½ to 1.
questions.concise: E ≈ αGb², α ≈ ½ to 1.
questions.detailed:
The dislocation strain energy per unit length is approximately:
```
E ≈ α G b² ,   with α ≈ ½ to 1
```
- (b) has the wrong exponent (Gb).
- (c) is a Frenkel-style expression, not the dislocation energy.
- (d) has b in the denominator — energy would *fall* with larger b, contradicting everything.
Two consequences follow directly (Q35): always pick the smallest b, and dissociate whenever
b₁² + b₂² < b².

questions.text: The b² dependence has two major consequences:

statements.text: dislocations always adopt the smallest available Burgers vector
a perfect dislocation can lower its total energy by splitting into two partials whose vector sum still equals the original b, provided b₁² + b₂² < b²
dislocations always adopt the largest Burgers vector
splitting always raises the energy

questions.keyExplanation: 1 and 2 correct; items 3 and 4 invert both consequences.
questions.concise: E ∝ b² ⇒ always the smallest b, and splitting into partials is favoured if b₁² + b₂² < b² — splitting *lowers* energy.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: dislocations always adopt the smallest available Burgers vector.
- Item 2 — TRUE: a perfect dislocation can lower its total energy by splitting into two partials
  whose vector sum still equals the original **b**, provided **b₁² + b₂² < b²**.
- Item 3 — FALSE: directly contradicts item 1.
- Item 4 — FALSE: splitting *lowers* the energy — that is why it happens.
Items 3 and 4 both invert the true consequences. The condition b₁² + b₂² < b² is the quantitative
test for whether dissociation is favourable — and it is satisfied in FCC.

questions.text: In FCC, the dissociation of a perfect dislocation is:
questions.concise: a/2[101̄] → a/6[21̄1] + a/6[112̄] — two Shockley partials.
questions.detailed:
In FCC the perfect dislocation dissociates into two Shockley partials:
```
(a/2)[101̄]  →  (a/6)[21̄1]  +  (a/6)[112̄]
```
**Verify it by vector addition:**
```
(a/6)[21̄1] + (a/6)[112̄] = (a/6)[2+1,  −1+1,  1−2]
                          = (a/6)[3, 0, −1]
                          = (a/2)[1, 0, −1]
                          = (a/2)[101̄]  ✓  matches the parent
```
**Verify the energy criterion (Q35):**
```
|b_perfect|² = (a/√2)²           = a²/2     = 0.500 a²
|b₁|² + |b₂|² = 2 × [(a/6)√6]²   = 2 × a²/6 = a²/3   = 0.333 a²

0.333 a²  <  0.500 a²  ✓  energy is lowered
```
- (b), (c), (d) either fail vector addition or violate the energy criterion.
**Always check both conditions** — vectors must sum correctly *and* energy must decrease.

questions.text: Between the two Shockley partials lies a ribbon of:

options.label: a
options.text: stacking fault — a region where the ABCABC… sequence is locally disrupted into an HCP-like ABAB… over a few atomic layers

questions.keyExplanation: Stacking fault — ABCABC locally becomes ABAB over a few layers.
questions.concise: Between the partials: a stacking fault where ABCABC is locally ABAB.
questions.detailed:
The region between the two Shockley partials is a **stacking fault** — a thin
ribbon where the normal FCC close-packing sequence is disrupted:
```
normal FCC:   ... A B C A B C A B C ...
with fault:    ... A B C A B A B C ...   (one layer misplaced → ABAB-like locally)
```
The fault has an associated **stacking-fault energy γ_sf** (per unit area), which is what
resists the ribbon widening (Q40).
- (b) a twin boundary is a *mirror-symmetric* region, several layers thick (Ch. 5 Q49) — different.
- (c), (d) are not what separates the partials.
The FCC→HCP analogy matters: HCP *is* the ABAB sequence, so a stacking fault is a thin slice of
HCP-like stacking inside an FCC crystal.

questions.text: Which statement(s) about stacking-fault energy (SFE) is/are correct?

statements.text: Low-SFE metals (brass, austenitic stainless steel) have wide partial-separated ribbons.
High-SFE metals (aluminium) have narrow ribbons, with the partials almost recombined.
A wide ribbon makes cross-slip difficult, because the partials must first constrict back together.
Low-SFE metals therefore work-harden *more slowly* than high-SFE metals.

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2, 3 correct. Item 4 is **false** — low-SFE metals work-harden *faster*. [P2]
questions.concise: Low SFE (brass, austenitic stainless) → wide ribbons → hard cross-slip — but they work-harden **faster**, not slower. Al has *high* SFE.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: low-SFE metals (brass, austenitic stainless steel) have wide partial-separated ribbons.
- Item 2 — TRUE: high-SFE metals (aluminium) have narrow ribbons, partials almost recombined.
- Item 3 — TRUE: a wide ribbon makes cross-slip difficult, because the partials must first
  **constrict** back into a perfect dislocation before it can switch planes.
- Item 4 — FALSE: low-SFE metals work-harden **faster**, not slower (see Q39).
- Item 4 also wrongly implies aluminium is low-SFE — Al is the standard *high*-SFE example.

**The chain to internalise:** low γ_sf → wide ribbon → cross-slip blocked → dislocations cannot
recover → **faster work hardening** and a planar dislocation structure. Every link matters.

questions.assertion: Low-stacking-fault-energy metals work-harden faster and retain a planar dislocation structure much longer than aluminium.
questions.reason: Wide partial ribbons impede cross-slip, which is the recovery mechanism that would otherwise let dislocations bypass obstacles and rearrange.

options.label: a
options.text: Both true, R correctly explains A

options.label: b
options.text: Both true, R does not explain A

questions.keyExplanation: Both true — wide ribbons block cross-slip, so recovery is suppressed.
questions.concise: Wide partial ribbons impede cross-slip — the very mechanism that would let dislocations recover — so hardening continues and the structure stays planar.
questions.detailed:
- A is TRUE: low-SFE metals work-harden faster and retain a planar dislocation structure much
  longer than aluminium.
- R is TRUE: wide partial ribbons impede **cross-slip**, which is the recovery mechanism that
  would otherwise let dislocations bypass obstacles and rearrange into lower-energy
  configurations (cells).

R correctly explains A. Aluminium, with narrow ribbons, cross-slips readily, recovers fast, and
therefore hardens more slowly and forms cell structures sooner. This connects Ch. 5 (SFE) to
Ch. 7 (work hardening, dynamic recovery).

questions.text: The equilibrium width of the stacking-fault ribbon is set by a balance between:

options.label: a
options.text: elastic repulsion of the two partials (widening) and the stacking-fault surface energy γ_sf (narrowing)

options.label: c
options.text: the grain size and the precipitate spacing

options.label: d
options.text: the vacancy concentration and the modulus

questions.keyExplanation: Partial repulsion widens; γ_sf narrows.
questions.concise: Partial repulsion widens the ribbon; γ_sf narrows it. Equilibrium = balance.
questions.detailed:
The equilibrium ribbon width is set by a balance of two opposing effects:
```
elastic repulsion between the two partials  →  pushes them APART (widens)
stacking-fault surface energy γ_sf          →  pulls them TOGETHER (narrows, since
                                               the fault has a positive energy per area)
```
At the equilibrium separation these exactly balance. So:
- **low γ_sf** → the fault is cheap → repulsion wins out → **wide ribbon**
- **high γ_sf** → the fault is expensive → pulls hard → **narrow ribbon**
- (b), (c), (d) are unrelated to the force balance.
This is the mechanical origin of everything in Q38 and Q39.

questions.text: Match the mechanism to the correct dislocation type and requirement.
tableRows: (a) screw; no diffusion; conservative; any temperature
(b) edge; needs vacancy diffusion; non-conservative; high temperature
questions.keyExplanation: Climb = edge, needs vacancies, non-conservative. Cross-slip = screw, no diffusion, conservative. [P2]
questions.concise: Climb = edge, needs vacancy diffusion, non-conservative. Cross-slip = screw, no diffusion, conservative.
questions.detailed:
| Mechanism | Type | Requirement |
|---|---|---|
| **Climb** | **edge** | needs vacancy diffusion; **non-conservative** (leaves the slip plane); thermally activated |
| **Cross-slip** | **screw** | **no diffusion**; **conservative** (stays in the plane of motion); possible at any temperature |

The mnemonic: **edge climbs** (it has a half-plane to absorb/emits vacancies), **screw
cross-slips** (it has no unique plane to be trapped in).
**[P2] the two-axis test:** (1) which dislocation type? (2) does it need diffusion?
Edge+diffusion = climb. Screw+no diffusion = cross-slip.

questions.text: Which statement(s) about dislocation interaction is/are correct?

statements.text: Like-sign dislocations repel.
Unlike-sign dislocations attract and annihilate if they meet on the same slip plane.
A Frank–Read source is a segment pinned at both ends that bows out, pinches off a loop, and regenerates the original segment.
Each Frank–Read cycle *reduces* the dislocation population.

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2, 3 correct. Item 4 is false — each cycle *adds* a loop.
questions.concise: Like-sign repel, unlike-sign attract/annihilate; Frank–Read pinches off loops and *regenerates* — so each cycle *adds* a dislocation.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: like-sign dislocations repel (their strain fields are of the same sign).
- Item 2 — TRUE: unlike-sign dislocations attract and, if they meet on the same slip plane,
  annihilate — leaving a perfect lattice.
- Item 3 — TRUE: a Frank–Read source is a segment pinned at both ends that bows out, pinches
  off a complete loop, and regenerates the original segment.
- Item 4 — FALSE: each cycle **increases** the dislocation population (it emits a loop), it does
  not reduce it.
Item 4 is the false member. The self-regenerating nature of the source is what allows dislocation
density to climb by four orders of magnitude during deformation.

questions.text: The Frank–Read source is the mechanism behind the huge rise in dislocation density during plastic deformation, from about:

options.label: a
options.text: 10⁶ cm⁻² in an annealed metal to 10¹⁰–10¹² cm⁻² heavily cold worked

options.label: b
options.text: 10¹² cm⁻² annealed to 10⁶ cm⁻² cold worked

questions.keyExplanation: 10⁶ (annealed) → 10¹⁰–10¹² cm⁻² (heavily cold worked).
questions.concise: 10⁶ (annealed) → 10¹⁰–10¹² cm⁻² (heavily cold worked).
questions.detailed:
Frank–Read sources drive the dislocation density up enormously during plastic
deformation:
```
annealed metal:            ~10⁶ cm⁻²
heavily cold worked:       10¹⁰ – 10¹² cm⁻²
```
That is a rise of **four to six orders of magnitude**. It is the microscopic basis of strain
(work) hardening in Ch. 7 — more dislocations means more mutual obstruction.
- (b) has the direction reversed.
- (c), (d) are far too small.
Note the units: **cm⁻²** (number crossing a unit *area*), because a dislocation is a line.

questions.text: In a dislocation pile-up against a barrier (grain boundary, hard precipitate):

options.label: a
options.text: the number of dislocations directly amplifies the local stress — the physical basis of Hall–Petch

questions.keyExplanation: More dislocations in the pile-up → larger local stress concentration → Hall–Petch.
questions.concise: More dislocations in a pile-up ⇒ larger local stress concentration ⇒ Hall–Petch.
questions.detailed:
When dislocations pile up against a barrier (grain boundary, hard precipitate),
they exert a repulsive force on each other, so the pile-up builds up. The stress concentration
at the **head** of the pile-up scales with the **number of dislocations** in it, n:
```
local stress at head ≈ n × (applied stress)
```
This amplified stress is what triggers slip in the neighbouring grain — and it is the physical
basis of the **Hall–Petch relationship** (Ch. 7).
- (b), (c), (d) are the opposite of what happens.
The key insight: a *longer* pile-up concentrates *more* stress, and a longer pile-up needs a
*bigger grain* to accommodate it — hence smaller grains are stronger (Ch.7 Q18).

questions.text: Dislocation multiplication matters because it:

statements.text: raises dislocation density during deformation
drives strain hardening (Chapter 7)
supplies the pile-ups that make grain boundaries strengthen (Hall–Petch)
softens the metal

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2, 3 correct; item 4 is the opposite.
questions.concise: Multiplication raises dislocation density, drives strain hardening, and supplies the pile-ups behind Hall–Petch — it strengthens, not softens.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: raises dislocation density during deformation (Q43).
- Item 2 — TRUE: drives strain hardening (Ch. 7 §7.1).
- Item 3 — TRUE: supplies the pile-ups that make grain boundaries strengthen (Hall–Petch, Q44).
- Item 4 — FALSE: it **hardens** the metal, it does not soften it.
Item 4 is the false member. This question shows how Ch. 5 (dislocation multiplication) feeds
directly into two of the four Ch. 7 strengthening mechanisms.

questions.assertion: Frank–Read sources operate under an applied shear stress and regenerate themselves.
questions.reason: Once the bowed wings meet behind the pinning points they annihilate, pinching off a complete loop while restoring the original pinned segment, ready to repeat.

options.label: a
options.text: Both true, R correctly explains A

options.label: b
options.text: Both true, R does not explain A

questions.keyExplanation: Both true — pinch-off plus regeneration is the self-feeding cycle.
questions.concise: Bowed wings meet behind the pins, annihilate, pinch off a loop, and restore the original segment — ready to repeat.
questions.detailed:
- A is TRUE: Frank–Read sources operate under an applied shear stress and regenerate themselves.
- R is TRUE: once the bowed wings meet behind the pinning points they annihilate, pinching off a
  complete loop while restoring the original pinned segment, ready to repeat.

R correctly explains A. The cycle:
```
apply stress → segment bows out → wings meet behind the pins → they annihilate
→ a complete loop is pinched off and runs away → the original pinned segment is restored
→ repeat
```
Each cycle adds one loop (Q42), which is why the source keeps producing dislocations until the
stress is removed or the loop encounters a barrier.

questions.text: Which statement(s) about a *grain boundary* is/are correct?

statements.text: It is the interface between two grains of different crystallographic orientation.
Low-angle boundaries (< 10–15° misorientation) can be modelled as an array of parallel edge dislocations.
High-angle boundaries are more disordered and have higher energy per unit area.
It is a mirror-symmetric, specific-angle reflection.

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2, 3 correct. Item 4 describes a *twin* boundary. [P2]
questions.concise: Grain boundary = interface between differently-oriented grains; low-angle = array of edge dislocations; high-angle = more disordered, higher energy — but it is *not* mirror-symmetric.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: it is the interface between two grains of different crystallographic orientation.
- Item 2 — TRUE: low-angle boundaries (< 10–15°) can be modelled as an array of parallel **edge
  dislocations** stacked one above another.
- Item 3 — TRUE: high-angle boundaries are more disordered and have higher energy per unit area.
- Item 4 — FALSE: "mirror-symmetric, specific-angle reflection" describes a **twin** boundary
  (Q48), not a random grain boundary.
Item 4 is a [P2] cross-contamination from the twin-boundary case.

questions.text: A *twin boundary* is:

options.label: a
options.text: a special, low-energy boundary across which the lattice is a mirror image of itself

options.label: b
options.text: the interface between two randomly oriented grains

options.label: c
options.text: a local error in the stacking sequence

options.label: d
options.text: the highest-energy defect in a crystal

questions.keyExplanation: Mirror-image lattice across the interface, low energy. [P2]
questions.concise: Twin boundary = mirror-image lattice across the interface, low energy.
questions.detailed:
A **twin boundary** is a special, low-energy boundary across which the lattice on
one side is a **mirror image** of the other. Because the atoms across it are in a coherent,
specific orientation relationship, the energy is much lower than a general grain boundary.
- (b) describes a *grain* boundary (random misorientation).
- (c) describes a *stacking fault* (Q49).
- (d) false — the twin boundary is one of the *lowest*-energy defects; the free surface is the highest (Q50).
**[P2] rule:** *grain = random misorientation; twin = mirror symmetry.* This is the exact pair
listed in your confusable-pairs table.

questions.text: Which statement(s) distinguish a *stacking fault* from a *twin boundary*?

statements.text: A stacking fault is a single missed or inserted layer in the stacking sequence.
A twin boundary is a mirror-symmetric region, typically several layers thick.
A stacking fault is bounded by two partial dislocations.
Both are identical in character.

questions.keyExplanation: 1, 2, 3 correct; item 4 is the trap. [P2]
questions.concise: Stacking fault = one missed/inserted layer, bounded by two partials. Twin = mirror region several layers thick. Not identical.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: a stacking fault is a single missed or inserted layer in the stacking sequence.
- Item 2 — TRUE: a twin boundary is a mirror-symmetric region, typically several layers thick.
- Item 3 — TRUE: a stacking fault is bounded by two partial dislocations (Q36, Q37).
- Item 4 — FALSE: they are *different* defects with different energies and origins.
**[P2] the distinguishing question:** *one mis-stacked layer (stacking fault), or a
mirror-symmetric region several layers thick (twin)?* The stacking fault is a 1-layer error
bounded by partials; the twin is a coherent mirrored region.

questions.text: Which statement(s) about the *external surface* as a defect is/are correct?

statements.text: It is technically the highest-energy defect of all, because surface atoms have unsatisfied bonds.
It is relevant to nucleation (Chapter 3) and to surface diffusion (Chapter 8).
It is the lowest-energy defect in a crystal.
Twin boundaries have higher energy than the free surface.

questions.keyExplanation: 1 and 2 correct; items 3 and 4 are both false (surface is the *highest*-energy defect).
questions.concise: The free surface is the *highest*-energy defect (unsatisfied bonds) and matters for nucleation and surface diffusion — not the lowest, and twin boundaries are lower.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: it is technically the highest-energy defect of all, because surface atoms have
  unsatisfied (dangling) bonds.
- Item 2 — TRUE: it is relevant to nucleation (Ch. 3 — surfaces provide heterogeneous sites) and
  to surface diffusion (Ch. 8 — the fastest diffusion path).
- Item 3 — FALSE: it is the **highest**-energy defect, not the lowest.
- Item 4 — FALSE: twin boundaries have *lower* energy than the free surface (item 1 already says
  the surface is the highest).
Items 3 and 4 both contradict item 1. **Energy ranking to remember:**
```
free surface  >  high-angle grain boundary  >  twin boundary / stacking fault  >  low-angle GB  >  perfect crystal (zero)
```
(The surface leads because its atoms have bonds reaching out into nothing.)
